newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France taxes big business to meet euro goal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France taxes big business to meet euro goal.

text.p: France's left-wing government slapped higher taxes on big business on Monday to bring down this year's public deficit after an audit showed it was running well above the target for a single European currency.

The audit ordered by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on taking office last month showed the 1997 deficit was running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, significantly beyond the three percent limit set by the Maastricht treaty.

To qualify for the euro, Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn announced steps to cut the deficit by 32 billion francs ($5.3 billion), with 22 billion in extra taxes on firms' profits and capital gains and 10 billion in spending cuts.

The measures won endorsement from Germany, France's chief partner in the drive to launch economic and monetary union in 1999. Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the French were doing their best to meet the Maastricht target.

Strauss-Kahn, who telephoned Waigel before announcing his package, refused to set a numerical target for the deficit in 1997, the reference year to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU), but said the measures "concern 0.4 percent of GDP".
"Less would have been insufficient, more would have blocked economic growth," he told a news conference. He also said the 1998 budget would limit the deficit to three percent.

France would meet the Maastricht treaty criteria "in the same conditions as its (European Union) partners", he said in a veiled reference to Germany's difficulties in achieving its own strict "3.0" percent interpretation of the treaty.
Economists said the measures could cut the French deficit to about 3.2 percent of GDP, sufficient to qualify for the euro.
In line with Jospin's campaign pledge that there would be "no new austerity" to qualify for EMU, the package contained no tax increase on households.

Financial markets reacted fairly calmly to the widely canvassed measures. The franc and bonds were steady but French shares were down 1.3 percent by midsession due to the slightly higher than expected corporate tax increase.
Strauss-Kahn said the defence budget would bear two billion francs of this year's 10 billion spending cuts.

Arguing that company profits were at a record high, and that previous centre-right governments had given industry tax breaks and subsidies, he announced a 15 percent surcharge on company tax in 1997 and 1998, falling to 10 percent in 1999.
The increases are calculated on the 33.3 percent basic rate of company tax. Corporate capital gains, taxed previously at 19 percent, will now be taxed at the same rate as profits.

The tax increase is on top of a 10 percent surcharge introduced in 1995 which took the effective tax rate to 36.6 percent. The new effective tax rate will be 41.6 percent this year and next year and 39.9 percent in 1999.
Small and loss-making firms were exempted from the increase.

The government said it was facing a tax shortfall this year of 15 to 17 billion francs and a public spending overshoot of 12 to 20 billion francs. In addition, the deficit in the main social security fund was running at 35 to 38 billion francs, compared with the 30.4 billion francs target forecast initially.

Speaking in Munich before Strauss-Kahn's statement, Waigel said the French were aware of their responsibilities and the tax rises were genuine measures, not creative accountancy, even though they should be followed by structural reforms.
Economists said the tax package was slightly bigger than expected but its concentration on big business was predictable.
"It is the corporate sector that takes the pain. The overall impact is slightly larger than people had been expecting," said Christopher Potts, economist at Paris brokers Cheuvreux de Virieu.

"All this is wholly coherent with the extremely Keynesian approach of the government," he said, referring to British economist John Maynard Keynes, who believed that government intervention could boost economic performance.
The centre-right opposition, ousted from office in a June 1 parliamentary election upset, attacked the government's emphasis on taxing business rather than cutting spending.

"The economic choices of the government go against the liberal policies which, throughout the world, allow growth and employment, via cuts in state spending, lower taxes and privatisations," said Alain Madelin, leader of the right-wing Liberal Democracy party.
"You can't be part of the euro game by swimming against the European tide," he said. ($= 6.041 French Francs)
